id: Poem to Some of My Recent Poems

prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

My beloved little billiard balls, my polite mongrels, edible patriotic plums, you owe your beauty to your mother, who resembled a cyclindrical corned beef with all the trimmings, may God rest her forsaken soul, for it is all of us she forsook; and I shall never forget her sputtering embers, and then the little mound. Yes, my little rum runners, she had defective tear ducts and could weep only iced tea. She had petticoats beneath her eyelids. And in her last years she found ball bearings in her beehive puddings, she swore allegiance to Abyssinia. What should I have done? I played the piano and scrambled eggs. I had to navigate carefully around her brain’s avalanche lest even a decent finale be forfeited. And her beauty still evermore. You see, as she was dying, I led each of you to her side, one by one she scorched you with her radiance. And she is ever with us in our acetylene leisure. But you are beautiful, and I, a slave to a heap of cinders.

prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: God, Yes, She

outputs.L1:
My beloved little billiard balls, my courteous mongrels, my edible patriotic plums: you owe your beauty to your mother, who resembled a cylindrical corned beef with all the trimmings. May God rest her forsaken soul, for it was all of us whom she forsook. I shall never forget her sputtering embers, and then the little mound.

Yes, my little rum-runners, she had defective tear ducts and could weep only iced tea. She had petticoats beneath her eyelids. In her final years, she found ball bearings in her beehive puddings and swore allegiance to Abyssinia. What was I to do? I played the piano and scrambled eggs. I had to navigate carefully around the avalanche of her brain, lest even a decent finale be forfeited.

And still, her beauty endures. You see, as she was dying, I led each of you to her side; one by one, she scorched you with her radiance. She remains ever with us in our acetylene leisure. But you are beautiful, and I am a slave to a heap of cinders.
outputs.L2:
My cherished small billiard spheres, my well-mannered mixed-breed darlings, my eatable plums of national devotion: your loveliness came from your mother. She looked like a tube-shaped corned beef served with every garnish; may God give peace to the abandoned soul of the woman who abandoned us all. I will always remember her crackling remains, and afterward, that modest grave-shaped rise in the earth.

Yes, my little smugglers of liquor, her tear ducts did not work properly, so the only thing she could cry was iced tea. Under her eyelids she carried petticoats. In the final period of her life, she discovered ball bearings inside her beehive puddings and declared loyalty to Abyssinia.

What was I supposed to do? I made music on the piano and beat eggs into confusion. I had to move cautiously around the landslide inside her mind, or else even a respectable ending might have been lost. Yet her beauty remained, and remains still.

You understand, when death was taking her, I brought each of you to her bedside in turn, and one after another she burned you with the force of her brilliance. She continues to stay among us during our acetylene hours of ease. But you are lovely, and I am bound in servitude to a pile of ashes.
outputs.L3:
The speaker addresses their children in a tone that is both affectionate and unsettling, speaking to them with tenderness while using strange, almost grotesque language. Their beauty is repeatedly traced back to their mother, as though she remains the source of whatever grace, charm, or radiance the children possess. Even in the speaker’s bizarre phrasing, there is a clear sense of love: the children are cherished, and their appearance becomes a living reminder of the woman who gave them life.

The mother herself is remembered as an extraordinary and deeply contradictory figure. She appears in memory as strange, luminous, and almost unreal, someone whose beauty and presence were impossible to separate from her instability and flaws. The speaker describes her in surreal physical and emotional terms, making her seem both human and mythic, both beloved and disturbing. She is radiant, but not peacefully so; her brilliance is tangled with suffering, eccentricity, and damage.

As the speaker recalls her decline and eventual death, the tone becomes a complicated mixture of grief, bewilderment, and dark humor. The memories are painful, but they are not presented with solemn simplicity. Instead, the speaker seems to cope with loss by turning it into something strange, sometimes absurd, and sometimes grimly comic. This dark humor does not erase the sorrow; rather, it shows how difficult the experience was to understand or endure. The mother’s deterioration appears to have been confusing, frightening, and emotionally exhausting for everyone around her.

The speaker also implies that they tried to manage her mental decline as best they could. There is a sense of responsibility in the way they remember caring for her, containing the chaos, and attempting to preserve some form of dignity despite the painful realities of her condition. Their efforts seem imperfect and strained, but sincere. They tried to protect her, the children, and perhaps even themselves from the full devastation of what was happening.

Even after her death, the mother’s presence continues to haunt the family. She is gone, but not absent. Her beauty lives on in the children, her strangeness remains in the speaker’s memories, and her suffering still shapes the emotional atmosphere of the household. The speaker remains devoted to her memory, unable or unwilling to let her disappear completely. In this way, the mother becomes a permanent figure in the family’s inner life: flawed, beloved, radiant, and unforgettable.
outputs.L4:
The speaker addresses his children directly, speaking to them as living reminders of the woman they came from. His voice moves through strange, comic, and surreal images, as if ordinary language is not enough to describe what their mother was or what happened to her. He remembers her beauty not as something simple or decorative, but as a force—brilliant, unsettling, almost unnatural. Her radiance seems to have filled the world around her, making her appear larger than life, yet that same intensity also foreshadows the suffering that will later consume her.

As the speaker recalls the mother’s decline, the tone shifts between tenderness, helplessness, and dark humor. Her mental and physical unraveling is presented through grotesque or absurd images, suggesting both the horror of her condition and the speaker’s desperate need to survive it by transforming pain into language. He cannot describe her illness plainly because plain description would not capture its strangeness or its cruelty. Instead, the surreal imagery becomes a way of showing how her deterioration distorted the family’s reality. The speaker watched the woman he loved become altered, diminished, and finally lost, while he himself struggled to remain present, to endure, and to care for the children left behind.

Yet the mother does not entirely disappear. Her beauty, though damaged by illness and ended by death, continues in the children. They have inherited her strange brightness, and the speaker sees in them the same radiance that once captivated and wounded him. This inheritance is both a gift and a burden. Their beauty connects them to their mother, preserving something of her that death could not erase, but it also binds them to the memory of her suffering. For the speaker, looking at his children means seeing both life and loss at once. They are proof that their mother’s presence survives, but they also keep him tied to grief, reminding him that what was most beautiful was also fragile, painful, and impossible to recover.
outputs.L5:
**God, Yes, She**

God is often spoken of as distant, powerful, and beyond all understanding. Yet sometimes, in the quiet moments of life, God feels close—like a gentle presence, a voice of comfort, or a hand guiding us forward.

And yes, there are many ways to imagine the divine. Some say “He,” some say “They,” and some say “She.” To call God “She” is to remember the tenderness, strength, wisdom, and creative power often associated with the feminine. She is the mother who nurtures, the spirit who listens, the light that remains when everything else feels dark.

God, yes—She can be found in compassion, in courage, in forgiveness, and in love. She is not limited by names or images. She is bigger than language, yet close enough to be felt in the heart.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a surreal, absurdist monologue by a grieving father addressing his children about their deceased mother, using grotesque affectionate nicknames and wildly incongruous imagery.
counterfactuals.output:
Children, my little chimney-swallows, my pudding-knuckled mooncalves, come sit by the radiator and listen to your father make a chandelier of his throat.

Your mother is dead.

There. I have said it plainly, like a shoe dropped into a soup tureen.

Your mother, my glorious cabbage-lantern, my velvet wart, my sweet cathedral of elbows, has gone where the clocks go when they are ashamed of ticking. She has stepped through the wallpaper and taken her enormous laugh with her. You know the one—the laugh that made teaspoons tremble, that caused pigeons to file complaints with the mayor, that could turn a Tuesday inside out and find a little golden button sewn into its lining.

Do not look at me like that, my beetle-bellies. I am still your father. I have merely misplaced the sky.

This morning I found her hairbrush on the dresser, still holding three silver hairs, three tiny ladders for ants who wish to ascend into heaven. I touched them and expected the room to sneeze her back into being. It did not. The room behaved disgracefully. It remained a room. Four walls, one ceiling, a window with the nerve to show me clouds.

Clouds! As if the world had not just lost its most ferocious duckling.

Your mother, my beloved pickle-saint, could scold a kettle into boiling. She could walk into a grocery store and come out with bread, plums, a screwdriver, and the secret sorrow of the cashier. She knew the private names of mildew. She once told me the moon was only a bruised knee belonging to God, and I believed her because she was wearing that red scarf and because I was young enough to think love was a kind of weather one could stand in forever without catching cold.

But now the house is full of her absence.

It sits in her chair with its legs crossed.

It uses her mug.

It hums badly in the kitchen.

Last night, my little jam-fisted goblins, I opened the cupboard and found all the plates facing backward, ashamed to be seen without her. The onions were weeping professionally. The salt had formed a union. Even the dog refused his dinner and stared at the corner where she used to stand, as though your mother might return as a committee of moths.

Perhaps she will.

Perhaps tonight, when you are asleep, your mother will come tapping at the window in the shape of a blue spoon. Perhaps she will rise from the garden, covered in marigolds and mortgage papers, and ask why no one has watered the basil. Perhaps she is already here, hiding in the breadbox, wearing crumbs for a crown, whispering, “Don’t let them leave their socks in the hall.”

And I will say, “My darling thunder-potato, my radiant bone-flower, I have failed in the matter of socks, but I am trying.”

I am trying, children.

I am trying to learn the machinery of mornings without her. The alarm clock screams like a goat in litigation. The toothpaste tastes of unpaid bills. Your lunches sit on the counter, small square coffins of peanut butter. I pack them anyway. I fold your shirts. I sign the school forms. I nod at neighbors who offer casseroles with the solemnity of diplomats delivering sealed declarations of war.

Everyone says, “She is in a better place.”

But what place could be better than here, where you are? Here, where the bathtub has claw feet like a nervous animal? Here, where the stairs creak out her name if you step on the third one sideways? Here, where her slippers remain under the bed, two soft boats waiting for a passenger who has missed the tide?

No. If there is a better place, it had better have your drawings on the refrigerator. It had better have the dent in the sofa shaped exactly like her tired body. It had better have you, my grubby cherubim, my magnificent little soup-stains, arguing over cereal while the sun spills itself stupidly across the table.

Listen to me.

Grief is not a straight road. It is a circus horse wearing your mother’s perfume. It is a fish with a telephone in its mouth. Some days it will sit gently beside you and knit. Some days it will burst through the ceiling dressed as a tax collector and demand everything shiny.

Let it come.

Do not be brave all the time. Brave is a coat that gets too hot. Cry in the cereal. Laugh at the funeral flowers. Ask dreadful questions. Tell me you miss her until the words are worn smooth as river stones. I will tell you I miss her too. I will tell you until my tongue becomes a tired red carpet leading nowhere.

And we will remember her badly and beautifully.

We will say she burned toast like an artist.

We will say she sang off-key with the confidence of a conquering emperor.

We will say she called you “my little turnips,” “my handsome mushrooms,” “my darling catastrophes,” and kissed your foreheads as if sealing envelopes addressed to the future.

We will keep her alive in the ridiculous ways. In the soup too full of pepper. In the birthday candles saved in a drawer though they are bent like old soldiers. In the way she danced when no music was playing, stirring invisible pudding with her hips.

Your mother is dead, my children.

But she is not gone like a dropped coin down a drain. She is gone like smoke into a coat. Like thunder into the bones of a house. Like a song swallowed by people who will hum it later without knowing why.

So come here, my little worm-crowned princes, my sugar-snouted gremlins. Let me hold you with these arms, these two bewildered branches. Let us sit together in the great pudding of evening.

We will be lonely.

We will be fed.

We will be strange.

And somewhere—inside the walls, inside the stars, inside the ridiculous surviving pump of my heart—your mother, my darling swamp-rose, my elegant disaster, my one true impossible bird, is laughing so hard the dead are complaining.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a short prose piece in the style of mid-century experimental fiction: a parent eulogizes his wife to their children with dark humor, non sequiturs, and strange domestic metaphors.
counterfactuals.output:
Children, your mother is now elsewhere, which is to say not in the kitchen, not in the blue chair, not correcting the television for its moral laziness. She has gone into that great municipal cupboard where all missing things are eventually shelved: umbrellas, teeth, promises, the good scissors.

Do not look so alarmed. Death is only a change of management. The body resigns; the furniture remains in office.

Your mother was a splendid woman, though not practical about pears. She believed they should be eaten at the exact instant between stone and soup, and she was usually right. She could make a bed as if negotiating a treaty. She could silence a room by entering it with a spoon. Once, during a snowstorm, she told a boiled egg it was being childish, and I agreed with her.

We will miss her in the usual places: at breakfast, beside the radiator, in the corridor where she stood like a small, reliable government. We will miss her where she was not, too—inside the linen closet, under the stamps, among the buttons in the jar, which now seem less like buttons than tiny closed mouths.

Do not think she has abandoned you. Abandonment requires planning, and your mother never planned anything without first making a list on the back of an envelope and losing it. No, she has merely stepped out of the house by a door we cannot find. Perhaps it is behind the pantry. Perhaps the pantry itself is the door.

When you are older, you will understand that love is a household appliance: dangerous when mishandled, impossible to replace, making an odd noise at night. Your mother kept us all humming. Now the house has gone very quiet, except for the clock, which is vulgar, and my heart, which is making soup in the basement.

So we shall be brave. We shall eat the pears before they accuse us. We shall fold the sheets into white, patient animals. We shall answer the telephone even when it is only the world, breathing.

And if you find her thimble, do not cry. Put it on the mantel. It is a small helmet. She was always going into battle with the curtains.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a bizarre literary paragraph that begins with “My beloved little billiard balls” and continues as an absurd elegy for the speaker’s dead spouse.
counterfactuals.output: My beloved little billiard balls, I whisper to the cataracted moon, you roll no more across the green felt of our marriage, no longer caroming gently against my ribs at supper, no longer clicking your ivory condolences from the pockets of the bed. Since my spouse was lowered into the earth—wearing the good hat, the one with the moths trained to sing hymns—I have dined only on chalk and funeral lilies, and every midnight I polish the cue of memory until it gleams like a bone persuading thunder. O darling, whose laugh could curdle the clocks, whose hands arranged the rain alphabetically, return to me as a soft collision, a white sphere of mercy, a numberless orb escaping the last dark pocket where all our kisses have been racked and waiting.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: I want a poetic, disturbing, funny speech where a widower tells his kids they got their beauty from their mother, whose illness and death are described through surreal images like food, machinery, and fire.
counterfactuals.output:
Kids, come here. Stand in the light a second.

No, not that light. The other one. The one coming through the kitchen window, bouncing off the toaster, making your faces look like they’ve been blessed by a very small, very confused angel who smells faintly of crumbs.

There. Look at you.

You got that from your mother.

Don’t argue. I know what’s mine. The ears are mine, unfortunately. The posture too—like a coat hanger that lost a bar fight. And the habit of opening the fridge, staring into it for three minutes, and then eating a pickle over the sink like a raccoon in a bathrobe. That is mine. I apologize for the pickle blood in the sink.

But the beauty? That’s hers.

Your mother was beautiful in a way that made mirrors nervous. They never knew what to do with her. They’d catch her face and then seem to say, “Oh. We should’ve polished.” She had eyes like the last two blueberries in the bowl—the ones everyone saves because they look important. She had a laugh like a drawer full of silverware being kicked down a staircase, and somehow it made the whole house feel set for dinner.

When she walked into a room, clocks took their hands off their faces and gave up. Plants leaned toward her like she was gossiping in sunlight. Even the kettle behaved better for her. For me it screams. For her it sang, like it had been waiting all its life to become steam.

And then—well.

Then came the thing.

The illness. I won’t name it tonight. Names are too small for monsters. Names make them sound like they can be introduced at parties. “Children, this is the thing that ate your mother’s Tuesdays first, then her appetite, then the staircase, then the little blue veins in her wrists.” No. It doesn’t get a name. Not at this table.

It came like a bad chef into the kitchen of her body. It opened every cupboard. It poured salt into the sugar jar. It curdled the milk of her sleep. It put knives where spoons should be. Her bones became breadsticks left too long in the oven. Her hands, those hands that could braid your hair, fix a torn hem, find a fever in the dark—those hands became pale little moths knocking at the window of herself.

Some days she was all flame.

Not dramatic flame, not movie flame, not the kind with brave music and a man running through a doorway carrying a child and, I don’t know, probably a dog. No. She was the flame inside a machine you are not allowed to open. The red whisper behind the boiler. The pilot light under the world. She burned quietly, behind panels, behind skin, behind the small polite smile she gave the nurse who could never get the vein on the first try.

And some days she was machinery.

Her breath clicked. Her bed hummed. Tubes looped around her like transparent garden snakes full of moonlight. The IV stand followed her everywhere, a skinny metal butler with wheels, holding up its little bag of ghost soup. The monitors blinked their green opinions. Beep, said the machine. Beep, said your mother’s heart. Beep, said I, because I didn’t know what else to contribute.

I brought her broth once. Homemade. I was very proud. It tasted like a chicken had wandered through hot water while thinking about onions. She took one spoonful and said, “Darling, if death has a flavor, you’ve made it beige.”

And we laughed. God help us, we laughed.

That was your mother too. Even when the illness had set up its awful carnival inside her, even when it was selling tickets to the collapse of everything, she could still point at the Ferris wheel and say, “Bit much, isn’t it?”

She got thin. I know you remember. Or maybe you don’t, and maybe that’s a mercy, or maybe memory is a dog that drags home whatever bone it wants.

She got so thin I was afraid the wind would solve her. I’d tuck the blanket around her and feel like I was wrapping a candle in a napkin. Her cheekbones became the handles of a drawer I couldn’t open. Her shoulders were two small hills after a fire. Her hair left slowly, like guests who don’t want to make a scene, gathering their coats one strand at a time.

But her beauty did not leave.

Listen to me.

Beauty is not prettiness. Prettiness is a cupcake with frosting. Beauty is the oven after the house has burned down, still warm enough to prove there was once bread. Beauty is the dented trumpet that can still wake the dead. Beauty is your mother looking at the ruin of herself and saying, “Well, this is inconvenient,” as if she had spilled tea on the apocalypse.

She was beautiful when she danced at our wedding and stepped on my foot so hard I saw a white door open in my brain.

She was beautiful when she was pregnant with you, swollen and furious, eating mustard on crackers at two in the morning and accusing me of breathing too loudly.

She was beautiful when she cut your sandwiches into triangles because, she said, rectangles were “bureaucratic.”

She was beautiful when she forgot the word for “lamp” and called it “the indoor sun on a stick.”

She was beautiful when she was dying, yes. I’m sorry. I know that’s a terrible thing to say. It sounds like putting a ribbon on a siren. But it’s true.

In those last days, she looked less like a person leaving and more like a match teaching darkness manners.

The room smelled of antiseptic, old flowers, and toast, because I kept burning toast. I don’t know why. Grief makes you incompetent at appliances. I would put bread in the toaster and then stare at the wall until the alarm went off and there it was: two black tablets from the Bible of Failure.

Your mother would whisper, “Again?”

And I’d say, “I’m experimenting.”

And she’d say, “With murder?”

And I’d say, “Mostly breakfast.”

And she’d smile. Not much. Just enough to keep the sun employed.

When the end came, it did not come like thunder. It came like the refrigerator stopping in the middle of the night. You know that sound? That sudden absence? The house holding its breath because the humming has quit? That was how she went. One moment the machine of her was working—clicking, laboring, heroic, absurd—and then it wasn’t.

No trumpets. No heavenly choir. No dramatic curtain. Just the soft click of some great invisible switch.

And the world, rudely, continued.

The kettle boiled. The mail came. Someone down the street ran a leaf blower, which I still consider an act of spiritual violence. A pigeon landed on the windowsill and looked in as if to say, “So, is anyone going to eat that toast?”

I wanted to scream. Instead, I threw away the toast.

That is marriage, children. That is grief. That is love at the end of its shift, sweeping crumbs from the counter while the universe pretends not to notice the missing queen.

But you—

Look at you.

You are the evidence she escaped.

Your faces are not copies. Don’t worry. You are not little museums of your mother, and I am not the old guard sleeping by the gift shop. You are yourselves. Strange, loud, expensive selves. You leave socks in places socks have no religious right to be. You drink juice directly from the carton like tiny warlords. One of you once asked if whales have knees and then cried because I did not know. You are ridiculous. You are alive.

And in each of you, she is not trapped. She is moving.

In your eyes, when you’re about to be kind and trying to hide it.

In your mouths, when you’re being sarcastic too young and too accurately.

In the way you stand close to people who are hurting, not knowing what to say, but standing there anyway—like a small lighthouse with no training.

That beauty? That’s hers.

She made it. She stirred it into you before you had names. She tucked it behind your ears. She baked it into your bones. She hammered it into the soft machinery of your hearts. She lit it like a stove in winter and said, “There. That should keep.”

So when you look in the mirror and feel awkward, or angry, or plain, or too much, or not enough—remember this: you are looking at a fire that survived its house.

And if sometimes that makes you sad, good. Let it. Sadness is not a hole. It is a room where love keeps its old furniture. Sit there when you need to. Put your feet on the table. Your mother would hate that, actually. Use a coaster.

But don’t stay forever.

Come back to the kitchen. Burn the toast. Laugh at the smoke alarm. Open the fridge and find nothing, then complain as if betrayed by a nation. Be beautiful in the ordinary, terrible way of living.

Because you got your beauty from your mother.

And she got it from somewhere even fire couldn’t reach.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4
